content: Bronchiectasis is a medical condition characterized by an abnormal and irreversible widening of the subsegmental airways. This condition can arise from a variety of underlying disease processes. Current treatment strategies for bronchiectasis include physiotherapy, antibiotics, and, in some cases, mucolytic agents. Many individuals with bronchiectasis are prescribed bronchodilator therapy because they often exhibit signs of airflow obstruction and bronchial hyper-responsiveness. However, the effectiveness of bronchodilator therapy in managing bronchiectasis has only recently begun to be systematically evaluated. The purpose of this review was to assess the effectiveness of short-acting beta-2 agonist therapy in individuals with bronchiectasis. This class of medication is the most commonly used treatment for addressing airflow obstruction in patients with this condition. To conduct this review, we searched the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register. Additionally, we reviewed the bibliographies of all identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to locate potentially relevant studies. The search was last updated in May 2008. We included all randomized controlled trials, whether single-blind or double-blind, in our selection criteria. The control group could consist of participants receiving a placebo, no treatment, or an alternative drug or physical therapy. Eligible participants included both children and adults who had been diagnosed with bronchiectasis through plain-film chest radiography, bronchography, or high-resolution computed tomography. Patients with cystic fibrosis were excluded from the review. Any form of short-acting beta-2 agonist, whether administered via inhalation or systemically, and used alongside conventional treatment, was considered for inclusion. Unfortunately, we were unable to extract or analyze data due to the absence of relevant RCTs. Our search identified 48 articles, most of which were excluded based on their abstracts because they were not RCTs. Six full-text articles were retrieved for further evaluation, but all were excluded after careful review because they either did not meet the criteria for being RCTs or did not address the specific research question. In conclusion, we did not identify any RCTs that investigated the role of short-acting beta-2 agonists in the treatment of bronchiectasis. Given that short-acting beta-2 agonist therapy is the most frequently used intervention for managing airflow obstruction in bronchiectasis, there is a clear need for future research to evaluate its effectiveness through well-designed RCTs.
